solution:
At the line where solid, liquid and air meet, the three interfacial tensions balance along the solid surface, so the angle of contact obeys

\(S_{LA}\cos\theta = S_{SA} - S_{SL}\),

where \(S_{LA}\), \(S_{SA}\) and \(S_{SL}\) are the liquid-air, solid-air and solid-liquid surface energies.

Water on glass: the adhesive attraction between water molecules and glass is stronger than the cohesive attraction among the water molecules themselves, so a water-glass interface is cheap to make and \(S_{SL} < S_{SA}\). Then \(\cos\theta > 0\), i.e. \(\theta\) is acute. In molecular terms the resultant force on a water molecule at the wall points towards the glass, the meniscus is concave and the liquid climbs the wall.

Mercury on glass: the cohesion between mercury atoms is far stronger than their adhesion to glass, so a mercury-glass interface is costly and \(S_{SL} > S_{SA}\). Then \(\cos\theta < 0\), i.e. \(\theta\) is obtuse. The resultant force on an atom at the wall now points into the mercury, the meniscus is convex and the liquid is pulled away from the wall.

Answer: because adhesion exceeds cohesion for water-glass, \(S_{SL} < S_{SA}\) and \(\cos\theta\) is positive, giving an acute contact angle; for mercury-glass cohesion far exceeds adhesion, \(S_{SL} > S_{SA}\) and \(\cos\theta\) is negative, giving an obtuse contact angle.

Whether a liquid spreads is settled by whether covering the solid lowers the total surface energy. Spreading destroys unit area of solid-air interface (energy \(S_{SA}\)) and creates unit area each of solid-liquid and liquid-air interface (energy \(S_{SL} + S_{LA}\)).

Water on clean glass: the water-glass adhesion is strong, so \(S_{SL}\) is small and \(S_{SA}\) is not less than \(S_{SL} + S_{LA}\). Spreading therefore lowers the energy, the angle of contact is small, and the water flattens into a film — it wets the glass.

Mercury on glass: mercury atoms attract one another far more strongly than glass attracts them, so \(S_{SL}\) is large and \(S_{SA} < S_{SL} + S_{LA}\). Spreading would raise the energy, so mercury minimises both its contact with the glass and its own free surface; its strong cohesion pulls it together into nearly spherical drops.

Answer: water wets glass because glass-water adhesion beats water-water cohesion, so spreading lowers the total surface energy; mercury does not wet glass because mercury-mercury cohesion far exceeds mercury-glass adhesion, so contracting into drops is the low-energy state.

Surface tension is defined as the force per unit length acting across an imaginary line drawn in the surface, equivalently the work needed to create unit area of fresh surface:

\(S = \dfrac{F}{l} = \dfrac{W}{\Delta A}\).

It originates in the unbalanced intermolecular attraction felt by the molecules of the few-molecule-thick surface layer, so its value is fixed by the nature of the two media in contact and by the temperature — nothing else.

Stretching the surface does not change the character of that layer: it merely brings more molecules up from the bulk into a surface layer identical to the old one, so each unit length of line in the surface still feels the same pull. \(S\) is therefore an intensive property, independent of how much area the surface has. (The total surface ENERGY \(S \times A\) does grow with area; the surface tension itself does not.)

Answer: because surface tension is a force per unit length — equivalently an energy per unit area — determined only by the two media in contact and the temperature, and enlarging the surface simply supplies more molecules to an unchanged surface layer without altering the pull per unit length.

Detergent molecules are surface-active: each carries a polar, water-attracting head and a non-polar, grease-attracting tail, so they collect at the interfaces rather than staying in the bulk. Adsorbed at the water-fabric interface they lower the solid-liquid surface energy \(S_{SL}\) sharply, and at the free surface they lower \(S_{LA}\) as well.

Since

\(\cos\theta = \dfrac{S_{SA} - S_{SL}}{S_{LA}}\),

reducing \(S_{SL}\) drives \(\cos\theta\) towards \(1\), that is, drives \(\theta\) towards zero.

This is exactly what washing needs. The capillary rise into the narrow spaces between the fibres of the cloth is \(h = \dfrac{2S\cos\theta}{\rho g r}\), which is large and positive only for a small \(\theta\). A solution with a large angle of contact would stand off the fabric instead of soaking into it and reaching the dirt.

Answer: the detergent lowers the solid-liquid surface energy, which raises \(\cos\theta\) and so makes the angle of contact small; and a small angle of contact is precisely the condition for the solution to wet the fabric and be drawn by capillarity into the fine spaces between its fibres.

solution:
With no external force acting, the only agent shaping the drop is surface tension, whose effect is to make the free surface as small as possible: the surface energy is \(U = S \times A\), and mechanical equilibrium is the state of least \(U\), hence of least area \(A\) for the fixed volume \(V\) of liquid.

Of all closed shapes enclosing a given volume, the sphere has the smallest surface area: for a sphere \(V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}\) and \(A = 4\pi r^{2}\), so \(A = \left(36\pi V^{2}\right)^{1/3}\), and no other shape of the same volume can do better than this.

Hence the drop settles into a sphere. It is only when an external force is present — gravity, for a large drop resting on a table — that the shape departs from spherical; a small drop, or a drop in free fall, is spherical.

Answer: surface tension minimises the surface energy and therefore the surface area at fixed volume, and the sphere is the least-area shape for a given volume, so a drop under no external force is spherical.

Surface tension is the extra energy per unit area carried by the surface layer, and that energy comes from the net cohesive attraction the surface molecules feel from the bulk.

Raising the temperature increases the mean kinetic energy of the molecules and increases their mean separation, so the cohesive attraction between them weakens. Less work is then needed to bring a molecule from the bulk up into the surface, and \(S\) falls. It goes on falling as the temperature rises and vanishes at the critical temperature, where liquid and vapour become indistinguishable and there is no surface left to have a tension.

Answer: decreases.

Blowing over the top raises the speed of the air above the sheet, while the air underneath stays essentially at rest.

For the air, Bernoulli's equation along a streamline at practically the same height gives

\(p + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^{2} = \) constant,

so where \(v\) is large \(p\) is small. The pressure just above the paper therefore drops below atmospheric by about \(\tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^{2}\), while the pressure just below it remains atmospheric.

The resulting upward pressure difference acting over the area \(A\) of the sheet gives an upward force \(\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^{2}\right)A\), which supports the weight of the paper and holds it horizontal.

If instead you blew underneath, the low-pressure region would be below the sheet and the net pressure force would push it downward.

Answer: blowing over the top speeds up the air there and so lowers the pressure above the sheet, leaving the full atmospheric pressure underneath to push it up and keep it horizontal; blowing underneath would lower the pressure below the sheet and press it down.

Let the hole have area \(a\) and lie at a depth \(h\) below the free surface of a liquid of density \(\rho\). The liquid leaves with Torricelli's efflux speed \(v = \sqrt{2gh}\), so the mass leaving per second is \(\dfrac{dm}{dt} = \rho a v\) and the momentum carried out of the vessel per second is

\(\dfrac{dp}{dt} = \left(\dfrac{dm}{dt}\right)v = \rho a v^{2} = 2\rho g h a\).

That rate of change of momentum is the forward force the vessel exerts on the escaping liquid. By Newton's third law the liquid exerts an equal and opposite force on the vessel, i.e. a backward thrust of magnitude \(2\rho g h a\).

The same result can be seen from the pressure distribution: while the vessel is closed the horizontal pressure forces on opposite walls cancel. Opening the hole removes the wall area that was being pushed outward on that side, while the pressure on the opposite wall is unchanged, so the horizontal forces no longer balance and there is a net force directed away from the hole.

Answer: the escaping jet carries momentum out of the vessel at the rate \(\rho a v^{2} = 2\rho g h a\), so by Newton's third law the vessel experiences an equal and opposite backward thrust of that magnitude.

Air is viscous, so a spinning ball drags the layer of air in contact with it around with itself. On the side of the ball whose surface is moving in the same direction as the oncoming air stream, this dragged air adds to the relative flow; on the opposite side it opposes the flow. The air therefore streams past one side of the ball faster than the other.

By Bernoulli's principle the faster side is at the lower pressure, so there is a net force on the ball directed from the slower, higher-pressure side towards the faster, lower-pressure side. This transverse force, perpendicular to the direction of motion, is the Magnus force.

A parabolic trajectory requires that the only force acting be the constant, vertically downward weight. Here the ball carries the Magnus force in addition to gravity, and that force changes direction as the ball's velocity turns, so the net force is neither constant nor purely vertical. The path therefore curves away from a parabola — the ball swerves.

Answer: spin drags air round with the ball, making the flow faster on one side than the other, so Bernoulli's principle gives a sideways pressure difference (the Magnus force). Acting in addition to gravity, this extra force means the resultant force is no longer a constant vertical one, and the trajectory is not a parabola.

No, it cannot.

Bernoulli's equation

\(p + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^{2} + \rho g h = \) constant

is derived on four assumptions: the flow is steady, the fluid is incompressible, the fluid is non-viscous so that no mechanical energy is dissipated, and the flow is streamline (laminar), the constant then holding along a streamline.

Water running through a rapid violates three of these. The flow is turbulent: the velocity at any point fluctuates rapidly and irregularly in time, so the flow is not steady, and there are no well-defined streamlines to apply the equation along. Eddies of every size form and break up, and viscous friction within them converts a large fraction of the mechanical energy into heat and sound.

Because that energy is genuinely lost from the flow, the quantity \(p + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^{2} + \rho g h\) decreases downstream instead of staying constant, so equating it at two points would give a wrong answer.

Answer: No — a rapid is unsteady and turbulent and dissipates mechanical energy through viscosity, so the steady, non-viscous, streamline conditions that Bernoulli's equation assumes do not hold and the quantity it asserts to be constant is not conserved.

No — it makes no difference, provided the same atmospheric pressure is subtracted at every point at which the equation is applied.

Write each absolute pressure as \(p = p_{g} + p_{0}\), where \(p_{g}\) is the gauge pressure and \(p_{0}\) the atmospheric pressure. Bernoulli's equation between two points becomes

\(\left(p_{g1} + p_{0}\right) + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_{1}^{2} + \rho g h_{1} = \left(p_{g2} + p_{0}\right) + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_{2}^{2} + \rho g h_{2}\).

The common constant \(p_{0}\) appears on both sides and cancels, leaving exactly the same equation written in gauge pressures. This is really the statement that only pressure DIFFERENCES enter Bernoulli's equation, and a difference is unchanged when the same constant is subtracted from both terms.

The one situation in which it does matter is when the two points are far enough apart — in practice, separated by a large enough height — for the atmospheric pressure itself to differ appreciably between them. Then the two constants are not equal, they do not cancel, and absolute pressures must be used.

Answer: No, it does not matter, because the atmospheric pressure is a constant added to both sides of the equation and cancels out; it matters only if the atmospheric pressures at the two points are significantly different.

The wing is essentially horizontal, so the \(\rho g h\) terms are the same above and below it and drop out of Bernoulli's equation. Taking the upper surface (speed \(v_{1} = 70\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), pressure \(p_{1}\)) and the lower surface (speed \(v_{2} = 63\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), pressure \(p_{2}\)),

\(p_{1} + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_{1}^{2} = p_{2} + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_{2}^{2}\),

so the excess of the pressure below over the pressure above is

\(\Delta p = p_{2} - p_{1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho\left(v_{1}^{2} - v_{2}^{2}\right)\).

With \(\rho = 1.3\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\):

\(\Delta p = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(1.3\right)\left(70^{2} - 63^{2}\right) = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(1.3\right)\left(4900 - 3969\right) = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(1.3\right)\left(931\right) = 605\,\text{Pa}\).

The lift is this excess pressure acting over the wing area \(A = 2.5\,\text{m}^{2}\):

\(F = \Delta p \, A = 605.15 \times 2.5 = 1.513 \times 10^{3}\,\text{N}\).

Answer: the lift on the wing is \(F \approx 1.5 \times 10^{3}\,\text{N}\), directed upward.

Both parts of the figure show the same horizontal tube — a wide section, a converging cone down to a narrow throat, then a diverging cone back to a wide section — with one vertical manometer tube standing on the wide part and a second standing at the throat. The two parts differ only in which of those two columns is the taller.

By the equation of continuity, \(A_{1}v_{1} = A_{2}v_{2}\), the speed at the narrow throat is GREATER than in the wide section, because the area there is smaller.

The tube is horizontal, so Bernoulli's equation reduces to

\(p + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^{2} = \) constant,

and therefore the pressure at the throat, where the liquid is moving fastest, must be the LOWEST pressure in the tube.

Each manometer column measures the pressure at its own foot through \(p = p_{0} + \rho g h\), so a lower pressure means a shorter column. The column standing at the throat must therefore be SHORTER than the one standing on the wide section. That is what the second of the two figures shows.

The first figure shows the taller column at the throat, i.e. the highest pressure at the point where the liquid is moving fastest. That contradicts Bernoulli's equation.

Answer: Fig. 9.20(a) is the incorrect one. It draws the liquid standing higher in the tube at the constriction, whereas the constriction is where the speed is greatest and hence the pressure least, so that column must be the shorter of the two — as drawn correctly in Fig. 9.20(b).
_note: Figure read off the rendered page scripts/ncert/out/c11PhyMechFluids/p-21.png (book p.201). In both panels one manometer tube stands on the wide section and one at the narrow throat; in (a) the throat tube carries the TALLER column, in (b) the wide-section tube does.

solution:
A soap film has TWO free surfaces, front and back, and each pulls on the slider along the whole of its length \(l\). The upward force on the slider is therefore

\(F = S \times 2l\).

The slider is in equilibrium under this force and the weight \(W\) hanging from it (which already includes the slider's own small weight), so

\(2Sl = W\), giving \(S = \dfrac{W}{2l}\).

Converting the length to SI, \(l = 30\,\text{cm} = 0.30\,\text{m}\), and with \(W = 1.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{N}\):

\(S = \dfrac{1.5 \times 10^{-2}}{2 \times 0.30} = \dfrac{1.5 \times 10^{-2}}{0.60} = 2.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{N m}^{-1}\).

Answer: the surface tension of the film is \(S = 2.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{N m}^{-1}\).

In all three parts of the figure the weight hangs from a horizontal slider of the SAME length, \(l = 40\,\text{cm} = 0.40\,\text{m}\); what differs between them is only the shape and the area of the film above that slider.

The film has two surfaces, and each pulls on the slider with a force \(S\) per unit length of the line along which it meets the slider. The upward force on the slider is therefore

\(F = 2Sl\),

and equilibrium requires the supported weight to be

\(W = 2Sl\).

This depends only on the surface tension and on the LENGTH of the slider. It does not contain the area of the film at all. The liquid and the temperature are the same in all three cases, so \(S\) is the same; the slider is \(40\,\text{cm}\) in all three, so \(l\) is the same; hence the supported weight is the same in all three.

Physically, this is because surface tension is a force per unit LENGTH and not a force per unit area. Enlarging the film does not make it pull any harder — it merely brings more molecules up from the bulk into a surface layer whose character is unchanged, so the pull on each unit length of the slider stays exactly the same.

As a check, the surface tension implied by the first case is \(S = \dfrac{W}{2l} = \dfrac{4.5 \times 10^{-2}}{2 \times 0.40} = 5.6 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{N m}^{-1}\), and this same value reproduces the weight in each of the other two.

Answer: the weight supported is \(4.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{N}\) in Fig. (b) and \(4.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{N}\) in Fig. (c) — the same as in Fig. (a) — because the supported weight is \(2Sl\), fixed by the \(40\,\text{cm}\) slider length and independent of the film's area.
_note: Figure read off the rendered page scripts/ncert/out/c11PhyMechFluids/p-21.png (book p.201). The three "40 cm" labels each mark the horizontal slider at the bottom of that frame; (b) is a taller rectangle than (a) and (c) has a gabled (pentagonal) top, so only the film AREA differs between the panels while the slider length is 40 cm throughout.

solution:
A mercury DROP is a body of liquid with a single free surface, the liquid-air interface, so the excess of the pressure inside over the pressure outside is

\(p_{\text{excess}} = \dfrac{2S}{r}\)

(not \(4S/r\), which applies to a soap bubble, whose thin film has two surfaces).

In SI units the radius is \(r = 3.00\,\text{mm} = 3.00 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}\), and \(S = 4.65 \times 10^{-1}\,\text{N m}^{-1}\):

\(p_{\text{excess}} = \dfrac{2 \times 4.65 \times 10^{-1}}{3.00 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{0.930}{3.00 \times 10^{-3}} = 310\,\text{Pa}\).

The pressure inside the drop is this excess added to the atmospheric pressure acting outside it:

\(p_{\text{in}} = p_{0} + \dfrac{2S}{r} = 1.01 \times 10^{5} + 310 = 1.0131 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\).

Answer:
excess pressure inside the drop \(= 310\,\text{Pa}\);
pressure inside the drop \(= 1.0131 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\), which to three significant figures is \(1.01 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\).

Part 1 — the soap bubble in air. A soap bubble is a thin film of liquid with TWO surfaces, an inner one and an outer one, each contributing \(2S/r\), so

\(p_{\text{excess}} = \dfrac{4S}{r}\).

With \(S = 2.50 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{N m}^{-1}\) and \(r = 5.00\,\text{mm} = 5.00 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}\):

\(p_{\text{excess}} = \dfrac{4 \times 2.50 \times 10^{-2}}{5.00 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{0.100}{5.00 \times 10^{-3}} = 20.0\,\text{Pa}\).

Part 2 — the air bubble inside the soap solution. Here there is only ONE surface, the single liquid-air interface separating the trapped air from the surrounding liquid, so the excess pressure is only half as large:

\(p_{\text{excess}} = \dfrac{2S}{r} = \dfrac{2 \times 2.50 \times 10^{-2}}{5.00 \times 10^{-3}} = 10.0\,\text{Pa}\).

The bubble sits at a depth \(h = 40.0\,\text{cm} = 0.400\,\text{m}\) in a liquid of relative density \(1.20\), i.e. \(\rho = 1.20 \times 10^{3}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\), so the pressure in the liquid just outside the bubble is

\(p = p_{0} + \rho g h = 1.01 \times 10^{5} + \left(1.20 \times 10^{3}\right)\left(9.8\right)\left(0.400\right) = 1.01 \times 10^{5} + 4.70 \times 10^{3} = 1.0570 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\).

The pressure inside the bubble exceeds this by \(2S/r\):

\(p_{\text{in}} = 1.0570 \times 10^{5} + 10.0 = 1.0571 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\).

Answer:
excess pressure inside the soap bubble \(= 20.0\,\text{Pa}\);
pressure inside the air bubble at a depth of \(40.0\,\text{cm}\) \(= 1.0571 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\), i.e. \(1.06 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}\) to three significant figures.
